Despite better alerts, dashboards, and analytics, retailers still face out-of-stock rates of 5% to 15%. BCG argues the bottleneck is no longer detecting empty shelves but connecting fragmented signals, diagnosing causes, and assigning action across the end-to-end supply chain.

Out-of-stocks are an ownership problem, not merely a data problemA gap can stem from forecasting, suppliers, distribution, ordering, or store execution. When no one owns the full outcome, alerts cascade to stores even when the root cause lies upstream.

Agentic AI turns isolated alerts into prioritized interventionsUnlike a conventional system that flags a problem, agents combine inventory, sales, supplier, logistics, and shelf data to identify likely causes, quantify value at stake, and direct action to the accountable owner.

Coordinated agents can prevent losses before shelves go emptyBCG’s Ava platform links specialized agents across supplier readiness, distribution, store inventory, and shelf execution. At one US retailer, it enabled proactive action on 70% of identified availability issues within a quarter.

Retailers should start with high-value failure modes, not a wholesale AI overhaulThe practical aim is to automate continuous detection and root-cause analysis while reserving human judgment for exceptions. Clarifying decisions, workflows, and ownership lets retailers build proactive availability management incrementally.

Retail has gotten better at filling the empty shelf over the past decade. Point-of-sale alerts, gap scans, inventory dashboards, exception reporting, computer vision, and increasingly sophisticated analytics can inform retailers when an item is unavailable, along with where the gap is occurring.Nonetheless, despite years of investment in forecasting, replenishment, and store execution, product availability remains a persistent challenge. While working with retailers, we have seen out-of-stock rates reach 5% to 15%, depending on the product category. Such gaps represent significant lost-sales opportunities, highlighting just how persistent the problem is.But identifying a problem is not the same as solving it. This is where agentic AI implementation redefines possibilities. Agents can connect signals across functions and systems, consider potential root causes, identify which owner is best positioned to act, and recommend or activate the next step. But how do those agents work together?BCG’s AVA system is one example of what agentic collaboration looks like in practice. It acts as a central coordinator that keeps the bigger picture in view. The system moves from signal to diagnosis to ownership to action, and it learns from each outcome for future planning, which should improve efficiency over time.Retailers Know What and Where; the Harder Question Is Why
The industry has invested heavily in mechanisms that detect availability gaps, but these tools are only effective up to a point: they reveal what is out of stock, where the issue is occurring, and when it began. Yet the deeper insight into the root cause, that is, the “why,” remains elusive.Consider a single out-of-stock. Is it a forecasting miss? Did the buyer order too little relative to demand? Did the supplier short the order? Was the product late to the distribution center? Did the store place the order correctly? Each possibility points to a different data source, process, system, and owner.This fragmentation creates a structural problem. Detection produces a barrage of signals, but a clear diagnosis often requires people to stitch together information across organizational boundaries. When the root cause is unclear, the issue rolls downhill to the store in the form of alerts, tasks, and exception lists. Store teams are asked to resolve the symptoms even when the actual cause may sit far upstream.Availability, therefore, should not be treated as a store metric alone. It is an end-to-end system outcome. (See Exhibit 1.)

Availability Is an Ownership Problem as Much as a Data Problem
The ownership challenge is visible both across the retailer enterprise and at the retailer-CPG interface. BCG’s work with manufacturers and retailers shows that availability gaps can persist despite years of data sharing and increasingly sophisticated forecasting.One reason is that accountability is distributed. A retailer buyer, replenishment planner, CPG sales analyst, supplier customer-service team, distribution operation, and store team may each own a piece of the process, but no single player owns the end-to-end outcome. The same pattern repeats at the store level: multiple teams can see part of the issue, but no one has the complete picture.More data does not solve that problem. What retailers need is a way to connect the signals, determine the most likely cause, and route the right action to the right owner. Historically, solving this problem at scale has been difficult for a simple reason: no single person, function, or system is chartered to reason continuously across the entire availability chain. Agentic technologies change that constraint.

Agents Can Close the Loop from Signal to Action
An availability agent with standing access to point-of-sale, inventory, forecast, vendor, logistics, planogram, promotion, and store-execution data can analyze those signals collectively rather than sequentially. A forecast miss can be evaluated alongside purchase orders and supplier delivery records. Store inventory can be interpreted alongside shelf conditions and labor or merchandising activity. Each signal becomes more useful because it is evaluated in context.This is the crucial difference between an alerting system and an agentic availability system. Instead of telling a user, “Here is a problem,” the system can say, in effect, “Here is the problem, here is the likely cause, here is the value at stake, here is the action required, and here is who should take that action.”AVA: From Individual Agents to an Integrated Availability Platform
Building a collection of disconnected AI pilots can only ever offer limited benefits. Real improvements in availability require coordination and an architecture in which specialized agents can connect into workflows, governance, and decision rights, creating a large enough perspective to operate against the common view of opportunity.BCG’s AVA is a modular suite of agents designed to convert fragmented retail signals into prioritized actions that improve product availability at shelf. AVA acts as the coordinating layer: identifying opportunities, quantifying their potential impact, diagnosing root causes, and routing actions into the appropriate workflows.The model has already produced results for a leading US retailer that previously identified availability issues only after sales were lost. Visibility into supplier and inbound performance was limited, while store-execution gaps could leave product in receiving or the backroom rather than on the shelf—until we deployed this AI-powered end-to-end approach to identify root causes.The AVA suite of agents assessed and evaluated availability risks before they resulted in lost sales. The solution connected supplier and DC readiness signals with store inventory and shelf-execution signals, then used closed-loop workflows to prioritize recovery actions and capture root-cause learning. Within one quarter, the retailer was able to proactively address 70% of identified availability issues. (See Exhibit 2.)

AVA allows different agents to address different parts of the availability system while working together. A supplier and DC readiness agent can monitor vendor inbound delivery and distribution-center inventory signals and route recovery actions before stores are affected. A store inventory and shelf execution agent can identify inventory that is physically in the store but not on the shelf, then prioritize execution based on sales exposure. A root cause and learning agent can quantify outcomes, identify recurring causes, and feed what worked back into planning and execution.The Destination: Proactive Availability Management
Retailers have more availability signals than ever, yet out-of-stocks remain persistent because the operating model around those signals is still fragmented. Upstream failures continue to become downstream store tasks. Root-cause analysis is often retrospective, and people spend substantial time reconciling systems before they can decide what to do.Agentic AI creates a different model, one in which availability is managed continuously across the system, issues are prioritized by value at stake, likely causes are diagnosed before becoming recurring failures, and actions are routed to the people and systems that can resolve them.Getting there does not require waiting for a perfect data environment or launching a massive transformation. Retailers can start process by process: identify the highest-value availability failure modes, define the decisions and actions required to address them, clarify ownership, and deploy agents where cross-system reasoning and coordination can materially improve outcomes.The goal should not be to automate every single availability decision. It should be to create a system in which machines do more of the continuous detection, synthesis, and root-cause reasoning, allowing people to focus on the exceptions and the decisions that require human judgment.Conclusion
The promise of agentic availability is not simply more intelligence, but a fundamentally tighter link between signal and action through contextualized support. When retailers treat availability as the system problem it has always been, agents can help turn fragmented data and diffuse ownership into coordinated execution at scale.
